cues.say: Those are rows in a Postgres database, on a server, somewhere else.
A username. A password stored as a hash that cannot be turned back into the password. A session token kept as a fingerprint rather than the token itself. And a comment, joined to a post by a key.
Twenty five minutes before this, none of it existed. One sentence built all of it.

say: This is lesson three, and it is the last one. We take the app from lesson two and give it the arrangement that real software actually runs on.

scene.title: A real website, a real database
scene.sub: One sentence turns a shared page into a hosted application with accounts, a database, image storage and a public address.

say: Start with why lesson two was not the end.

cues.say: This is where lesson two finished. A real address, one shared feed, everybody seeing the same posts.
It works. For six friends it is genuinely enough, and I would not talk you out of it.
But every post, every like and every comment is stored inside the page itself, and that is the ceiling.

say: Three things break when you grow. The page carries all its own content, so it gets heavier with every post. Two people acting at the same moment can overwrite each other. And there are no real accounts, just a name you typed.

items.name: It gets heavier
items.note: Every photo lives inside the page. Everybody downloads all of them.

items.name: People collide
items.note: Two at once, and the last one wins. The other is gone.

items.name: No real accounts
items.note: A name you typed is not a login.

say: The fix is the same one nearly every application you use is built on. Move the content out of the page and into a database, put the page on a server that talks to it, and give people real accounts.

panels.what: One page holding everything. Simple, and it does not scale past a group chat.
A server, a database, real accounts, and photos stored separately.

say: One sentence asks for all of it.

cues.say: Same window as the first two lessons, same folder, nothing new installed.
This only works for a few friends. I want it on a real website with a proper database.
Notice the first half. I named the limitation I had hit, in my own words, before asking for anything.
That is the sentence. No hosting company named. No database named. No mention of accounts, or storage, or any of what is about to appear.

say: Naming the limitation is the trick worth taking from this whole course. It only works for a few friends is a fact about your situation, and it tells the tool what the finished thing has to survive. Ask for a database and you get a database. Say what is going wrong and you get an answer to that.

chunks.text: this only works for a few friends
i want it on a real website with a proper database
chunks.tag: where you want to get to

say: Then it goes to work, and the choices are the lesson.

cues.say: Twelve times speed. In real time this is twenty minutes and almost none of it needs your eyes.
It rebuilds the whole application properly rather than bolting a database onto the old one. Real pages, real routing, a login screen, a signup screen.

And here is the thing worth stopping for. It builds the entire app and tests it before it has a database at all. The screens render, the login gate correctly turns visitors away. Only then does it go looking for somewhere to store things.
That ordering is not an accident. Prove the shape works, then wire in the thing that is slow to change.
It also quietly updated three libraries past security advisories, including one that allowed database injection. Nobody asked. It just read the warnings.

say: That last one deserves a sentence of its own. One of the versions it started with had a known hole that would let somebody send commands to your database through an ordinary form. It upgraded past it without being asked and mentioned it in passing.

scene.title: The thing nobody asked for
scene.name: It patched a security hole
scene.tagline: Found in a dependency, upgraded, mentioned in passing
facts: In a library it had just installed.
Fixed before anybody could have noticed.

cues.say: Now the only moment in three lessons where it genuinely could not continue on its own. It needs a database, and a database needs an account somewhere.
So it stops and lays out four routes, with the trade off of each one. Sign in properly. Paste a key. Take a temporary one now and claim it later. Or something else.
It recommends one, and it says why, and it waits.

Then it works something out for itself. The account is managed through the hosting company, so the ordinary route will not work, and it switches to the other path. Its words. That is the cleaner production setup anyway.

say: This is the pattern to expect whenever real accounts and money are involved. It will get you to the edge of what it can do alone, explain the options in plain language, and stop. That is not a failure. That is the right behaviour, and answering takes ten seconds.

scene.title: When it stops and asks

steps.name: It will not sign you up for things
steps.note: Accounts and money need you. Correctly.

steps.name: It lays out the routes
steps.note: With the trade off of each, in plain words.

steps.name: You pick, in a few words
steps.note: Then it carries on. Usually ten seconds of your time.

sweepAt: could not continue on its own

say: And then in about a minute it has a Postgres database, a set of tables designed for this app, and seven demo accounts with eight posts already in them, so the thing has something to show the first time you open it.

items.name: Seven accounts, eight posts
items.note: So it is not empty when you first look.

say: Then it puts it on the internet properly.

cues.say: Fourteen times speed through the rest, which is half an hour of testing and fixing.

It finds that double tapping to like was impossible, because a single tap navigated away first. It finds that pages crashed for signed out visitors. It finds that the icon buttons had no names a screen reader could announce.
None of those were reported by me. It found all three by using its own application.
It also handles photographs properly now. An upload is resized and stored separately from the page, so the feed stays light no matter how many people post.
And then it deploys, and the build takes sixteen seconds.
Here is what it reports, and the interesting part is the shape of it.

A list of everything it verified on the live site rather than only on this laptop. Signing up, logging in, posting, liking, commenting, following, deleting, uploading a two megabyte photograph, search, notifications, dark mode, and the phone layout.
And then the one thing it could not verify, named exactly. A load more button that only appears past twelve posts, and there are ten.
Three lessons in, that habit is the single best signal you have that a tool is worth trusting.

say: So let us go and use it like a stranger would.

cues.say: A public web address. Not a file, not a shared document. A website.
And it does not let me straight in. It asks who I am, which is what a real account looks like.
A real signup form. An email, a name, a username, and a password with a minimum length it will enforce.
And a line underneath that somebody thought about. Your username is yours, and nobody else can post under it.
I am filling this in as an obvious test account, because everything I type is about to become a permanent row in a real database.
And that is a real account, created against a real Postgres database, on a public website, by somebody who did not write any of it.
Straight into the feed. Those posts are not in the page. They came out of the database when the page loaded.
A like. One becomes two.
And a comment. Hello from a real database.
In lesson two that comment would have rewritten and republished the entire page. Here it goes into a table and touches nothing else.
But you should not take my word for that, and neither should you take the app’s word for it. So let us go and look.

say: Ask it to show you the actual data.

cues.say: I just signed up as demoviewer on the live site and commented on a post. Show me that in the database.
And there it is. A row in a table called users, stamped with the second it was created.

Look at the password. It is not there. What is stored is a hash, which is a one way scramble. The app can check a password against it and can never turn it back into one. If somebody stole this entire table they still would not know what I typed.
The session is the same idea. What is kept is a fingerprint of the login token, not the token. The real one only exists in my browser.
And the comment, in its own table, joined to the post by a key. Four columns. That is the whole write.
It also notes, without being asked, that the email I invented is now a real row in a live database, and that if this app ever sends password reset mail, it will go there.

say: That password detail is worth more than the rest of this video. A well built application does not know your password. It stores a scramble, checks new attempts against it, and cannot reverse it. Nobody asked for that. It is simply what building it properly means.

panels.what: A one way scramble. Useless to a thief. Enough to check a login against.
Your password. The app never knew it and cannot find out.

say: And there is the difference between the three lessons in one line. Lesson one wrote to your own browser. Lesson two rewrote the whole page every time anybody did anything. Lesson three writes four columns to a table and nothing else on the site notices.

steps.name: Lesson one
steps.note: Saved in your browser. Gone if you open it anywhere else.

steps.name: Lesson two
steps.note: The entire page rewritten and republished. Everyone shares it.

steps.name: Lesson three
steps.note: Four columns into a table. Nothing else touched.

say: So where does this leave you.

You have a hosted application with real accounts, a real database, image storage and a public address, and it cost nothing to start. Three sentences got you here, one per lesson, and not one of them contained a technical word.

scene.title: Three sentences, three lessons

steps.name: put this on the internet
steps.note: An address, and one shared feed.

steps.name: i want it on a real website with a proper database
steps.note: Accounts, a database, and photo storage.

sweepAt: not one of them contained a technical word

say: Be clear about what this is not. It is not finished, it has no paying customers, and nobody has tried to break it. But it is the same arrangement the applications on your phone are built on, and you can now change it by asking.

panels.what: The real arrangement. Server, database, accounts, storage, an address.
A tested product. Nobody has used it in anger or tried to break it yet.

say: And the skill you actually learned has nothing to do with databases. You learned to say what you want in your own words, to say what is going wrong when it goes wrong, and to read the part at the end where it tells you what it could not check.

scene.title: The whole course, as three habits

items.name: Say what you want
items.note: Plainly. In your words. Name the limit you hit.

items.name: Say what you see
items.note: When it breaks, describe it. Do not diagnose it.

items.name: Read the last paragraph
items.note: Especially the part about what it could not verify.

say: That is the course. Built it, shared it, and made it real.
Go and build the thing you have been meaning to build. You now know everything you need to start, and the rest you can ask for.

lines: You never wrote a line of it.
